challenges.judge_assessment: The statutory-definition point is real but the attack overreaches. R.C. 5321.01(A) supports the proposition that Chapter 5321 tenant status ordinarily requires entitlement under a rental agreement. It does not establish that every person outside that definition may be removed by self-help, or that Chapter 1923 is limited to statutory tenants. R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) separately reaches an occupier without color of title when the complainant has the right to possession, and the brief invokes that broader language plus Sutherland. Thus appellees can substantially weaken the R.C. 5321.15 theory by showing no rental agreement, but the cited sources do not dispose of the Chapter 1923/occupier theory. The advocate risks losing the statutory landlord-tenant remedy, including statutory damages and fees, unless she establishes a rental agreement or a distinct rule barring self-help against this kind of occupant.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if Alice did not qualify as a tenant under R.C. 5321.01(A), appellees still could not remove her by changing the locks. R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) and (6) authorize forcible-entry-and-detainer proceedings against an occupier of lands or tenements and against unlawful detention of those premises. The undisputed point is that appellees resorted to self-help instead of the process Ohio law requires.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that Alice was a 'tenant' unless you can point to a rental agreement; instead say the record shows she was at least an occupier of Edwin's residence, and R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) and (6) required appellees to use forcible-entry-and-detainer process rather than self-help. If you want to keep the Chapter 5321 theory, you need facts establishing tenant status; the supplied record does not show them.

challenges.opponent_argument: R.C. 5321.15 prohibits a 'landlord' from excluding a 'tenant' by self-help. Because Alice was not a tenant, Edwin was not a landlord under R.C. 5321.01(B), and the statute does not apply. (Source 22, 25). Moreover, the common law permits a property owner to exclude a licensee without judicial process. The brief's reliance on Coward v. Fleming and other authority is misplaced because those cases involve landlord-tenant relationships, not a homeowner and a houseguest.
challenges.why_it_matters: The self-help claim under R.C. 5321.15 fails as a matter of law, removing a key basis for the wrongful ouster claim.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands strongly against the brief's specific reliance on R.C. 5321.15. Sections 5321.15 and 5321.01 expressly regulate acts by a landlord against a tenant, and the present record identifies no rent, lease, or other rental agreement. The brief calls Alice a social guest, consort, house companion, and occupant at Edwin's will, none of which by itself satisfies the statutory definition. But the attack's additional assertion that common law permits summary exclusion of a licensee is unsupported by Sources 22 and 25, and its characterization of Coward is likewise unsubstantiated by the retrieved material. The court could therefore reject the R.C. 5321.15 theory without deciding whether Chapter 1923 or common law independently prohibited the lockout. The advocate stands to lose the clearest statutory damages-and-fees route, not necessarily every ouster theory.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees contend that R.C. 5321.15 cannot apply because Alice was not a tenant. But that concession does not make the lockout lawful. At minimum, appellees were required to resort to the forcible-entry-and-detainer process before excluding Alice from the residence; changing the locks and posting notices was self-help, not lawful process.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that R.C. 5321.15 is vulnerable without a rental agreement and do not rest the brief on it unless the record can show tenant status. The cleaner path is to argue that self-help lockout was improper and that Chapter 1923 was the required procedure.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even if Alice were considered an 'occupier' under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), that statute merely provides a cause of action for forcible entry and detainer; it does not create a private right of action for damages for self-help exclusion. The brief cites no authority that a violation of Chapter 1923 gives rise to a tort claim for wrongful ouster. The proper remedy for a person wrongfully excluded is to seek restitution under Chapter 1923, not to sue for damages in a separate action. Thus, the trial court correctly dismissed the ouster claim.
challenges.why_it_matters: This challenges the legal basis for the entire wrongful ouster claim, suggesting it is not cognizable as a separate tort.

challenges.judge_assessment: This identifies a substantial remedial gap. R.C. 1923.02 describes when forcible-entry-and-detainer proceedings may be brought; the cited statutory source does not itself establish a damages action by an excluded occupant. The brief moves from the proposition that appellees should have used Chapter 1923 to the conclusion that Alice has a damages claim for wrongful ouster, without identifying the cause of action, its elements, or authority recognizing it outside R.C. 5321.15. The attack goes too far in asserting that restitution is necessarily the exclusive remedy, because Source 4 does not say that. Still, unless the complaint and Ohio common law supply an independent wrongful-eviction, trespass, conversion, or quiet-enjoyment claim, proving that Chapter 1923 was the proper possession procedure may not itself support damages. The advocate risks losing the standalone ouster claim even if the lockout was procedurally improper.
challenges.suggested_response: Chapter 1923 does not authorize appellees to resort to self-help. Rather, it confirms that possession was to be regained through statutory process, not by changing the locks and barring Alice from her belongings. That unlawful exclusion is relevant because appellees then retained Alice's property and never returned it, supporting her separate conversion claim.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not imply that Chapter 1923 itself creates a damages action. Use it only to show appellees were required to proceed by judicial process, and tie the damages claim to conversion or any other pleaded common-law theory that the complaint actually contains.

challenges.why_it_matters: This factual admission undermines the legal classification essential to her ouster claim.

legal_sources.citation: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law, 2022-06 (Sixth Edition), XIII. Tenant Claims for Seizure of > C. Additional Remedies (PDF pp. 512–514)

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a meaningful challenge to the conversion element, but it understates the record. Alice's affidavit allegedly says identified belongings remained in the house, appellees kept them, and they were never returned; the repeated lock changes and notices allegedly prevented her from retrieving the balance. A jury could treat deliberate exclusion while retaining known property as control inconsistent with her possessory rights even without use, sale, or destruction. Source 31 recognizes conversion as an available common-law claim in the seizure context but does not establish that denial of access is insufficient. The brief's conclusory statement that it was 'obvious' Cathryn knew of the property is vulnerable, especially as to each appellee's knowledge and control, but the cited source does not justify judgment as a matter of law. The advocate risks losing conversion if the affidavit does not competently show ownership, appellees' knowledge and control, and an actual denial of retrieval.
challenges.suggested_response: The summary-judgment record does more than show a denial of access. Alice swore that she left personal property in the residence, including suits, dresses, craft materials, and papers, and that appellees kept those items and never returned them. A jury could find that conduct to be wrongful control or exercise of dominion over property belonging to another and inconsistent with Alice's rights.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Expand the conversion discussion to emphasize the affidavit's averments that appellees kept the identified items and never returned them. Avoid arguing only from denial of access; instead frame the repeated lockouts and continued retention as evidence of dominion inconsistent with Alice's rights.

attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This highlights a missing element that the brief did not address, supporting summary judgment.

judge_assessments.assessment: The statutory-definition point is real but the attack overreaches. R.C. 5321.01(A) supports the proposition that Chapter 5321 tenant status ordinarily requires entitlement under a rental agreement. It does not establish that every person outside that definition may be removed by self-help, or that Chapter 1923 is limited to statutory tenants. R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) separately reaches an occupier without color of title when the complainant has the right to possession, and the brief invokes that broader language plus Sutherland. Thus appellees can substantially weaken the R.C. 5321.15 theory by showing no rental agreement, but the cited sources do not dispose of the Chapter 1923/occupier theory. The advocate risks losing the statutory landlord-tenant remedy, including statutory damages and fees, unless she establishes a rental agreement or a distinct rule barring self-help against this kind of occupant.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief concedes Alice occupied at Edwin's will or sufferance, argues that revocation made her a tenant at sufferance under Sutherland, and separately relies on R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) and (6), which refer to occupiers and unlawful detention rather than only tenants.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The text and facts of Sutherland v. Moore, and Ohio authority distinguishing a gratuitous co-occupant or licensee from a tenant at will or sufferance, would settle whether Alice's status required judicial process.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands strongly against the brief's specific reliance on R.C. 5321.15. Sections 5321.15 and 5321.01 expressly regulate acts by a landlord against a tenant, and the present record identifies no rent, lease, or other rental agreement. The brief calls Alice a social guest, consort, house companion, and occupant at Edwin's will, none of which by itself satisfies the statutory definition. But the attack's additional assertion that common law permits summary exclusion of a licensee is unsupported by Sources 22 and 25, and its characterization of Coward is likewise unsubstantiated by the retrieved material. The court could therefore reject the R.C. 5321.15 theory without deciding whether Chapter 1923 or common law independently prohibited the lockout. The advocate stands to lose the clearest statutory damages-and-fees route, not necessarily every ouster theory.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief invokes R.C. 5321.15, labels Alice a tenant at sufferance after permission was revoked, and argues under Coward and Chapter 1923 that even such a tenant may be ejected only by statutory process. It does not identify a rental agreement.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research whether an implied rental agreement can arise from nonmonetary consideration or the parties' course of conduct, and obtain Coward v. Fleming's actual holding and factual setting.

judge_assessments.assessment: This identifies a substantial remedial gap. R.C. 1923.02 describes when forcible-entry-and-detainer proceedings may be brought; the cited statutory source does not itself establish a damages action by an excluded occupant. The brief moves from the proposition that appellees should have used Chapter 1923 to the conclusion that Alice has a damages claim for wrongful ouster, without identifying the cause of action, its elements, or authority recognizing it outside R.C. 5321.15. The attack goes too far in asserting that restitution is necessarily the exclusive remedy, because Source 4 does not say that. Still, unless the complaint and Ohio common law supply an independent wrongful-eviction, trespass, conversion, or quiet-enjoyment claim, proving that Chapter 1923 was the proper possession procedure may not itself support damages. The advocate risks losing the standalone ouster claim even if the lockout was procedurally improper.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Chapter 1923 afforded Alice protection and that Edwin could regain possession only through forcible-entry-and-detainer process; it also invokes R.C. 5321.15 damages and fees. It does not separately define or cite authority for a common-law wrongful-ouster damages claim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complaint's pleaded causes of action and Ohio appellate decisions recognizing or rejecting damages for common-law wrongful eviction of a licensee, occupant, or tenant at sufferance are needed. Research also whether Chapter 1923 is exclusive as to possession but permits collateral tort damages.

judge_assessments.assessment: The record supports the absence of an express rental agreement or rent payment, and that is damaging to statutory tenant status under R.C. 5321.01(A). But the attack misstates the brief by saying u16 and u17 admit Edwin later revoked permission; u17 concerns illness and a power of attorney, while revocation is a legal inference from the lockout and notices. More importantly, absence of a rental agreement does not by itself negate the brief's separate classification as an occupier under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5). On this record the attack can defeat or seriously impair the Chapter 5321 theory, but cannot establish that no protected possessory status existed as a matter of law. The advocate risks having the court separate and reject the statutory-tenant label while still considering the broader occupier theory.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Alice moved in at Edwin's request, lived there with him, and was at least a social guest; the brief characterizes her occupancy as at will or sufferance and argues it became a tenancy at sufferance when Edwin ended it. No rent or rental agreement is alleged.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The summary-judgment affidavits and exhibits should be examined for evidence of shared expenses, services, remodeling contributions, or other consideration capable of supporting an express or implied rental agreement.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a meaningful challenge to the conversion element, but it understates the record. Alice's affidavit allegedly says identified belongings remained in the house, appellees kept them, and they were never returned; the repeated lock changes and notices allegedly prevented her from retrieving the balance. A jury could treat deliberate exclusion while retaining known property as control inconsistent with her possessory rights even without use, sale, or destruction. Source 31 recognizes conversion as an available common-law claim in the seizure context but does not establish that denial of access is insufficient. The brief's conclusory statement that it was 'obvious' Cathryn knew of the property is vulnerable, especially as to each appellee's knowledge and control, but the cited source does not justify judgment as a matter of law. The advocate risks losing conversion if the affidavit does not competently show ownership, appellees' knowledge and control, and an actual denial of retrieval.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies suits, dresses, craft materials, and papers; says Alice repeatedly entered to recover belongings but was locked out again; states appellees kept the remaining items and never returned them; and argues those circumstances constitute dominion inconsistent with her rights.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the exact affidavit language, the defendants' affidavits, and Ohio appellate authority on conversion by withholding access to chattels left on premises, including whether active use or disposition is necessary.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source does not support the assertion that demand and refusal are invariably essential elements of Ohio conversion. Demand and refusal are generally evidence of conversion when the defendant's initial possession was lawful; they are unnecessary when other acts already amount to wrongful dominion. Here the brief alleges direct exclusion, known retrieval attempts, retention, and nonreturn, which could supply the requisite adverse exercise of control. The court would not affirm on a categorical demand requirement without authority and analysis addressing whether appellees' possession began lawfully. This attack should be discarded as unsupported and overly absolute.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief does not allege a formal verbal or written demand and refusal, but it alleges Alice repeatedly attempted to reclaim her property, was locked out, and that appellees kept and never returned the remaining items.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Obtain controlling Ohio appellate authority distinguishing conversion by an initially lawful possessor from conversion by an independently wrongful act.

judge_assessments.assessment: This largely repackages a1 and adds an unsupported common-law proposition. Sources 8 and 25 address the Chapter 5321 definition of tenant; they do not establish that a homeowner may use self-help against every licensee or that R.C. 1923.02(A)(5)'s broader occupier language is inapplicable. It also treats Alice's disputed legal status as conclusively established rather than addressing the brief's Sutherland and occupier arguments. The court should not accept this as an independent basis for affirmance on the supplied authority.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges Alice was at least a social guest but argues her established residence, occupancy at Edwin's will, subsequent status as a tenant at sufferance, and R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) protection required process.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The same research identified for a1 would determine the status issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abstract statement that legal insufficiency can support summary judgment is correct, but this attack does not demonstrate a Dresher-compliant motion on the actual record. Sources 8 and 25 define tenant; they do not show what appellees' motion specifically identified or negate Alice's alternative status as an occupier under Chapter 1923. Nor does the brief claim that any immaterial factual dispute defeats judgment; it states the conventional essential-element standard. The court would apply de novo review, but this proposed framing adds nothing beyond the tenant-status attacks and assumes the dispositive conclusion.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the dispute must concern an essential element and asks whether the evidence is sufficiently disputed or so one-sided that one party must prevail. It also argues appellees failed to affirmatively identify an absence of evidence and that Alice supplied an affidavit and exhibits.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The appellees' summary-judgment motion and supporting Civ.R. 56 materials are necessary to evaluate compliance with Dresher.

results.verdict: partially persuasive on the lockout theory, but exposed on t
results.assessment: The brief reads well on the core fairness point: appellees changed the locks and excluded Alice rather than using process, and the conversion theory has some factual support from the retained belongings. But it is vulnerable where it most needs legal footing. The Chapter 5321 tenant theory is shaky because the record does not show a rental agreement, and the Chapter 1923 argument does not itself supply a damages cause of action. The conversion count is also vulnerable if the affidavit does not clearly show ownership, control, and denial of retrieval. The research leaves open whether an independent wrongful-ouster claim exists outside those statutes.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands forcefully against the R.C. 5321.15 theory. That statute protects a statutory “tenant” from self-help by a “landlord,” and R.C. 5321.01 ties both statuses to a rental agreement. The record described in the brief shows cohabitation at Edwin’s invitation but identifies no lease, rent, or other rental agreement. The brief labels Alice a tenant at sufferance without connecting that label to Chapter 5321’s definition. The court could therefore affirm summary judgment on the R.C. 5321.15 claim. But appellees would overreach by treating this as dispositive of every claim: Chapter 1923 may reach some nontenant occupiers, and conversion is independently governed by property law.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant does not contend that R.C. 5321.15 is independently established on this record if the Court concludes there was no rental agreement. The summary-judgment record does, however, show that appellees changed the locks, posted notices excluding appellant, and retained her property. Those facts independently create genuine issues under Chapter 1923 and on conversion, and they preclude summary judgment even if the Court declines to apply Chapter 5321.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that the record does not show the rental agreement needed to invoke R.C. 5321.15, and either delete the statute-specific paragraph or recast it as an alternative argument contingent on a Chapter 5321 tenancy. The stronger, record-supported theories are Chapter 1923 and conversion.

challenges.why_it_matters: If Alice is not a tenant, the entire claim that the lockout was an unlawful ouster under Chapter 1923 fails, and summary judgment was proper.

challenges.judge_assessment: The cited sources support the narrower proposition that Alice may not be a “tenant” under Chapter 5321 without a rental agreement. They do not support the broader assertion that Chapter 1923 governs only landlord-tenant relationships. R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), which the brief invokes, expressly concerns an “occupier” without color of title, and Chapter 1923 is not textually confined to statutory tenants. Thus the attack conflates Chapters 5321 and 1923 and does not defeat u54 as framed. There remains a genuine weakness in the brief—whether Alice’s invited cohabitation made her an occupier at will or sufferance and whether Chapter 1923 supplied the exclusive removal process—but this attack’s cited authorities do not resolve it. Pressing the categorical tenant-only argument risks leaving the brief’s actual subsection (A)(5) theory unanswered.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if appellees are correct that the present record does not establish a rental agreement under Chapter 5321, that does not end the case. R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) and (6) authorize forcible-entry-and-detainer relief against an occupier who unlawfully detains premises, and appellees' own evidence shows that Cathryn repeatedly changed the locks and excluded appellant from the residence. Chapter 1923 is therefore implicated by the facts alleged here regardless of whether appellant can be labeled a Chapter 5321 tenant.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise paragraph 31 to stop treating Chapter 5321 as the governing source of relief and to anchor the lockout argument in R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) and (6). Do not say Chapter 1923 is limited to formal tenants unless you can point to a rental agreement in the record; the safer point is that the statute reaches an occupier and unlawful detention of the premises.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief fails to establish the essential element of conversion: wrongful exercise of dominion over property. The mere fact that Alice was locked out and could not retrieve her belongings does not show that the appellees actively controlled, used, or disposed of her property. Conversion requires more than denial of access; it requires an affirmative act inconsistent with the owner's rights. The brief's own cited authority (Kraft, Joyce) defines conversion as 'wrongful control or exercise of dominion,' yet the facts alleged show only that the locks were changed, not that the appellees exercised control over the items.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without conversion, Alice cannot recover any damages, including nominal damages, and summary judgment on that claim was appropriate.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack understates the record and is not supported by source 61. Alice’s affidavit evidence, as recounted in the brief, was not merely that her belongings happened to remain inside: she said appellees knew she was retrieving them, repeatedly changed the locks, prevented further retrieval, kept the remaining property, and never returned it. Viewed in her favor, those facts can support an inference of control inconsistent with her ownership rights. Source 61 recognizes conversion as a possible remedy for seizure or withholding of a tenant’s property; it does not establish the proposed rule that denial of access cannot constitute dominion. The brief may not conclusively establish conversion, but at summary judgment it need only create a genuine issue. Appellees would risk asking the court to draw factual inferences against the nonmovant.
challenges.suggested_response: Viewed in appellant's favor, the summary-judgment evidence supports a finding of conversion. Appellees knew appellant had personal property in the residence, knew she was attempting to recover it, repeatedly changed the locks to prevent further access, and never returned the remaining suits, dresses, craft materials, and personal papers. That evidence permits a reasonable inference of wrongful control or exercise of dominion over property belonging to another, and at minimum creates a jury question. If conversion is found, appellant is entitled at least to nominal damages.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the conversion claim, but support it with the specific facts showing withholding and continued control: repeated lock changes, notices barring entry, appellant's sworn statement that appellees kept her remaining belongings, and the failure to return them. Avoid a bare conclusion; make the jury-inference point explicit.

attacks_proposed.argument: Alice was not a 'tenant' under Ohio law because she had no rental agreement with Edwin. R.C. 5321.01(A) defines a tenant as 'a person entitled under a rental agreement to the use and occupancy of residential premises to the exclusion of others.' The brief admits Alice lived with Edwin as a consort or house companion, not under a lease. Therefore, she was a mere guest or licensee, not entitled to the protections of R.C. Chapter 1923, which governs landlord-tenant relationships.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Alice is not a tenant, the entire claim that the lockout was an unlawful ouster under Chapter 1923 fails, and summary judgment was proper.

attacks_proposed.argument: R.C. 5321.15 prohibits self-help only by a 'landlord' against a 'tenant.' Because Alice was not a tenant and Edwin was not her landlord—there being no rental agreement—the lockout did not violate that statute. The brief's reliance on R.C. 5321.15 is misplaced; the statute simply does not apply to this non-landlord-tenant relationship.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The statutory basis for the wrongful exclusion claim collapses, removing the foundation for liability and damages under R.C. 5321.15.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief fails to establish the essential element of conversion: wrongful exercise of dominion over property. The mere fact that Alice was locked out and could not retrieve her belongings does not show that the appellees actively controlled, used, or disposed of her property. Conversion requires more than denial of access; it requires an affirmative act inconsistent with the owner's rights. The brief's own cited authority (Kraft, Joyce) defines conversion as 'wrongful control or exercise of dominion,' yet the facts alleged show only that the locks were changed, not that the appellees exercised control over the items.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without conversion, Alice cannot recover any damages, including nominal damages, and summary judgment on that claim was appropriate.

attacks_proposed.argument: The appellees did not merely make conclusory assertions; they pointed to the absence of a rental agreement and Alice's status as a guest, which negated an essential element of her claims—the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship. Under Dresher, a movant can meet its initial burden by demonstrating that the nonmoving party lacks evidence on a specific essential fact. The appellees did exactly that, and the trial court correctly found no genuine issue.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the movants met their burden, the summary judgment was procedurally sound and should be affirmed.

attacks_proposed.argument: The argument for nominal damages is contingent on establishing conversion. Because the brief fails to prove conversion—as shown by the lack of evidence of wrongful dominion—Alice is not entitled to even nominal damages. The cited case Scales v. Progressive Builders only applies once conversion is established, which it is not.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The damages claim fails entirely, removing any basis for a jury trial on that issue.

attacks_proposed.argument: The trial court did not err because Alice failed to produce evidence on essential elements of her claims, such as the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship or wrongful dominion over her property. The brief's claimed factual disputes are not genuine; they rest on a misapplication of law that would not entitle her to relief. Summary judgment was therefore proper, and the decision should be affirmed.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The appeal should be denied, and the dismissal of Alice's complaint should stand.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands forcefully against the R.C. 5321.15 theory. That statute protects a statutory “tenant” from self-help by a “landlord,” and R.C. 5321.01 ties both statuses to a rental agreement. The record described in the brief shows cohabitation at Edwin’s invitation but identifies no lease, rent, or other rental agreement. The brief labels Alice a tenant at sufferance without connecting that label to Chapter 5321’s definition. The court could therefore affirm summary judgment on the R.C. 5321.15 claim. But appellees would overreach by treating this as dispositive of every claim: Chapter 1923 may reach some nontenant occupiers, and conversion is independently governed by property law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Alice was an occupant at Edwin’s will or sufferance, that even a tenant at sufferance must be removed through statutory process, and that R.C. 5321.15 prohibited her exclusion. It does not identify a rental agreement or analyze R.C. 5321.01’s tenant definition.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The historical 2005 versions of R.C. 5321.01 and 5321.15, the statutory definition of “rental agreement,” and Ohio authority addressing whether an invited cohabitant can qualify under an oral or implied rental agreement would settle the precise scope.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited sources support the narrower proposition that Alice may not be a “tenant” under Chapter 5321 without a rental agreement. They do not support the broader assertion that Chapter 1923 governs only landlord-tenant relationships. R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), which the brief invokes, expressly concerns an “occupier” without color of title, and Chapter 1923 is not textually confined to statutory tenants. Thus the attack conflates Chapters 5321 and 1923 and does not defeat u54 as framed. There remains a genuine weakness in the brief—whether Alice’s invited cohabitation made her an occupier at will or sufferance and whether Chapter 1923 supplied the exclusive removal process—but this attack’s cited authorities do not resolve it. Pressing the categorical tenant-only argument risks leaving the brief’s actual subsection (A)(5) theory unanswered.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief characterizes Alice as an occupant at will or sufferance, cites R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) and (6), and relies on Coward for the proposition that a tenant at sufferance may be ejected only through forcible-entry-and-detainer process.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The historical text and construction of R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), plus Coward v. Fleming and Ohio cases involving removal of invited cohabitants or licensees, would determine whether Alice falls within Chapter 1923 and whether its remedy was exclusive.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack understates the record and is not supported by source 61. Alice’s affidavit evidence, as recounted in the brief, was not merely that her belongings happened to remain inside: she said appellees knew she was retrieving them, repeatedly changed the locks, prevented further retrieval, kept the remaining property, and never returned it. Viewed in her favor, those facts can support an inference of control inconsistent with her ownership rights. Source 61 recognizes conversion as a possible remedy for seizure or withholding of a tenant’s property; it does not establish the proposed rule that denial of access cannot constitute dominion. The brief may not conclusively establish conversion, but at summary judgment it need only create a genuine issue. Appellees would risk asking the court to draw factual inferences against the nonmovant.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief defines conversion as wrongful control or dominion inconsistent with the owner’s rights and asserts that appellees knew Alice had property inside, knew she was attempting to recover it, repeatedly locked her out, kept the remaining items, and never returned them.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Authority addressing demand and refusal when possession was initially lawful could refine the analysis, but the proposed attack neither cites such authority nor accounts for the affidavit’s assertion that the property was kept and never returned.

judge_assessments.assessment: This cannot be credited on the supplied record. Nothing provided from appellees’ summary-judgment motion shows that they specifically identified the absence of a rental agreement or supported that contention with Civ.R. 56 materials. Source 18 concerns legally insufficient eviction notice and does not establish Dresher’s burden or what appellees actually argued. Even if appellees made the proposed showing, it would address the Chapter 5321 theory, not necessarily Chapter 1923’s occupier provision or conversion. The brief also expressly argues that appellees merely asserted lack of proof and submitted evidence admitting that Edwin directed Alice’s removal. Without the motion and supporting materials, the attack assumes the decisive procedural fact.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says appellees claimed generally that Alice could prove no facts, failed to affirmatively negate a specific essential fact, and submitted Edwin’s affidavit acknowledging that he directed Cathryn to remove Alice.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual summary-judgment motion, Edwin’s affidavit, and all accompanying Civ.R. 56 materials are necessary to determine whether appellees satisfied Dresher on each claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal premise is correct but adds no independent basis for affirmance: nominal damages are available only after conversion is established. The brief itself states that condition. The attack therefore succeeds only if the separate conversion attack succeeds, and on this record Alice’s affidavit creates at least a triable question of wrongful control or withholding. Source 61 does not negate conversion or address Scales’s nominal-damages rule. Appellees gain nothing by treating the conditional damages proposition as an independent defect.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says, quoting Scales, that nominal damages are available “once conversion has been established,” and argues that the evidence establishes or at least permits a finding of conversion.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full text of Scales would confirm the nominal-damages rule, but the disposition turns principally on whether the conversion evidence creates a genuine issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a conclusion assembled from the other attacks rather than an independent procedural objection. Source 18 does not support the asserted summary-judgment analysis. The absence of a rental agreement may defeat the R.C. 5321.15 theory, but it does not by itself dispose of the broader Chapter 1923 contention or conversion. The assertion that there is no evidence of wrongful dominion also misreads Alice’s affidavit allegations that appellees knowingly prevented retrieval, kept the property, and never returned it. A court could affirm individual claims on narrower grounds, but this attack does not justify affirmance of the entire dismissal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies sworn evidence of repeated lock changes, directives not to enter, Edwin’s instruction to remove Alice, belongings remaining inside, frustrated retrieval attempts, and appellees’ retention and nonreturn of those belongings.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Claim-by-claim review of the complaint, the summary-judgment motion, and the trial court’s stated grounds would be required before concluding that every cause of action fails.

results.verdict: Mixed but vulnerable on the statutory theory; the factual co
results.assessment: As written, the brief is not yet persuasive on its central statutory theory because it leans hard on R.C. 5321.15 even though the record described shows no rental agreement, so the tenant/landlord premise is exposed. It is also vulnerable where it treats Chapter 1923 as if it applied only to landlord-tenant relationships; that overstates the law and leaves the actual occupier-at-will/sufferance theory underdeveloped. The brief is stronger on conversion, because the challenged record can support an inference of wrongful control when appellees knew appellant was trying to retrieve her property, changed the locks, and never returned it. The research does not resolve whether Chapter 1923 is the exclusive removal process on these facts.

elements.explanation: The brief describes the condition as lead paint hazards in the walls, ceilings, floors, dust, and soil at the East 53rd Street property. It also gives dates showing the condition and dispute persisted over time, but it does not expressly narrate the full duration in one place.

elements.label: The landlord was given notice of the condition
elements.requirement: The brief says the landlord knew or was told, and when.
elements.explanation: The brief alleges Stark had actual notice after a city inspection and received notices and orders to correct the lead condition, with dates attached. That is enough in the supplied text to show notice was pleaded and supported by the brief's cited allegations.
elements.quote: "upon information and belief, Third party Defendant Stark Group, LLC was on notice that the property on East 53rd was contaminated with lead paint after an inspection by the city on or about November 18th, 2004"; "failed to correct the lead paint condition ... even though they received several notices and orders to correct this condition from the City of Cleveland"; "Appellee Stark received an order on February 2, 2005 to control the lead hazards identified at 3420 E. 53rd St."

elements.label: The landlord had a reasonable opportunity to repair
elements.requirement: The brief accounts for the time between notice and the filing.
elements.explanation: The brief gives a compliance deadline and extension, then says Stark later sold the property instead of abating the hazard. That supplies a time period between notice and the later filing/sale sufficient to plead an opportunity to repair.
elements.quote: "Appellee Stark received an order on February 2, 2005 to control the lead hazards identified at 3420 E. 53rd St. Despite agreeing to comply and receiving an extension to comply with the order until May 14, 2005, failed to abate the nuisance and instead walked away from the property"; "instead sold the property on E. 53rd ... on November 17th 2006"

elements.label: The consequence the tenant claims is stated
elements.requirement: The brief says what follows from the breach -- abatement, a defense to possession, damages -- and ties it to the duty it identified.
elements.explanation: The brief ties the breach to negligence per se, proximate cause of the child's injuries, and a request for monetary and punitive damages and attorney fees. It therefore states what follows from the alleged breach and links that consequence to the cited duty.
elements.quote: "Appellee's failure to comply with the order requiring it to abate the lead nuisance ... is negligence per se"; "the trial court erred in not finding this intentional and willful refusal to comply with the law to be both the factual and proximate cause of Ashoura's physical and emotional injuries"; "The Carters' Third Party Complaint was brought to seek monetary damages, punitive damages, and attorney fees for violations of failure to disclose, warn or correct lead paint"

challenges.opponent_argument: Ohio has not adopted Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 840A or 373 for lead-paint nuisance claims against former owners. The 8th District has held that a seller is divested of all obligations upon transfer of title. Steele v. McNatt, 102 Ohio App.3d 558, 562 (8th Dist. 1995). The out-of-state cases cited by Appellants are not binding and do not reflect Ohio law. The trial court correctly concluded that Stark's liability ended when it relinquished ownership, particularly through a foreclosure sale.

challenges.judge_assessment: The central point lands: the brief concedes that no Ohio decision has adopted or applied Restatement §§ 840A or 373 to this situation, and its principal supporting decisions are nonbinding cases from other jurisdictions. That leaves Appellants asking the Eighth District to recognize a materially expanded former-owner duty. But the attack overstates Steele as categorically terminating every liability upon transfer. Source 73 itself signals a qualification involving defective conditions left unremedied at the time of sale, and a transfer ordinarily does not extinguish liability that accrued from the transferor's own earlier tortious conduct. Section 373 also appears directed to harm outside the land, making it a questionable fit for occupants injured on the premises. The lack of controlling Ohio authority is nevertheless a serious obstacle, and if the court declines to adopt the proposed Restatement rule, the common-law theory fails.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants acknowledge that no Ohio decision has expressly adopted Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 840A or 373 in this precise context. But the complaint does not depend on a broad Restatement expansion alone. It alleges that Stark knew of the lead hazard, received a lawful order to abate it, failed to remedy the condition, and transferred the property while the hazard remained. Source 73 recognizes that Ohio law does not necessarily end the inquiry merely because title has passed when the seller has failed to remedy defective conditions at the time of sale. At minimum, those allegations state a continuing-nuisance and negligent-maintenance claim that should not have been dismissed on the pleadings.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede the absence of controlling Ohio authority on Restatement §§ 840A and 373, and use them only as persuasive support for a narrower Ohio nuisance/continuing-defect theory. Tie the argument to the pleaded allegations that Stark knew of the hazard, was ordered to abate it, failed to do so, and transferred the property with the condition unresolved.

challenges.opponent_argument: The statutes and ordinances Appellants rely on for negligence per se do not impose a duty on a former owner who is no longer a landlord. R.C. 5321.04 applies only to a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement. Stark was not the Carters' landlord. The lead hazard control order issued under C.C.O. 240.04(e) and R.C. 3742.37 obligated Stark while it owned the property, but upon transfer, those obligations do not run to subsequent tenants. Ohio law holds that a seller is divested of all rights and obligations upon transfer of title. Steele v. McNatt, 102 Ohio App.3d 558, 562 (8th Dist. 1995). Therefore, no statutory duty existed at the time of the Carters' tenancy, and the negligence per se claim fails as a matter of law.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a statutory duty, the negligence per se theory collapses, and the trial court's dismissal of that claim was correct.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack lands strongly as to R.C. 5321.04: the statutory text quoted by the brief applies to a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement, and Stark was not the Carters' landlord during their tenancy. Shroades and Sikora therefore do not by themselves extend that statute's negligence-per-se duty to later tenants after title has passed. The attack is less conclusive as to the lead-control order and Cleveland ordinance. The alleged violation occurred while Stark owned the property, and transfer does not necessarily erase liability for an already completed statutory breach merely because injury occurred later. Steele, at least as presented in source 73, does not establish the attack's categorical proposition, and source 73 indicates a possible qualification for defects left unremedied at sale. Still, the brief cites no controlling Ohio authority holding that these lead-abatement provisions create a tort duty running from a former owner to subsequent occupants. That missing legal bridge is a substantial merits problem.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not rely on R.C. 5321.04 as the only source of duty. The Third Party Complaint alleges that Stark received the City’s lead-hazard control order on February 2, 2005, was given time to comply, and nevertheless failed to abate the nuisance before transferring the property. The complaint further alleges that C.C.O. 240.04(e) made compliance with the Commissioner’s order mandatory and that Stark’s noncompliance was the breach that led to the continuing hazard affecting subsequent occupants. At the pleading stage, those allegations are sufficient to state a claim based on Stark’s own failure to obey a lawful abatement order and to keep the premises free from a known hazardous condition.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the statutory-duty argument. Do not rest the claim on R.C. 5321.04 alone; instead emphasize Stark’s alleged violation of the lead-hazard control order and Cleveland ordinance while it owned the property, and frame the question as whether that pleaded breach can survive dismissal despite later transfer.

challenges.opponent_argument: The trial court's failure to convert the motion or rule on the Civ.R. 56(F) request was harmless because the legal question of whether Stark owed a duty to the Carters after transferring the property could be resolved without further discovery. Under Ohio law, a seller is divested of all obligations upon transfer of title. Steele v. McNatt, 102 Ohio App.3d 558, 562 (8th Dist. 1995). Thus, even if the motion had been treated as one for summary judgment and additional discovery allowed, Appellants could not establish a duty, and the outcome would be the same.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the error was harmless, the appellate court will affirm despite the procedural irregularity, and Appellants gain no relief on this assignment of error.

challenges.judge_assessment: A harmless-error argument is available, but this version depends entirely on establishing as a matter of law that no post-transfer duty could exist. Source 73 does not support that categorical premise; its snippet quotes Steele's divestiture language but immediately identifies a qualification or unresolved issue when a selling landlord has already failed to remedy a statutory defect. The record also indicates that the trial court affirmatively relied on the foreclosure manner of transfer, a fact different from the pleaded direct sale. If that fact was outside the pleadings, the court could not use it while granting Civ.R. 12(B)(6) relief without following the appropriate conversion procedure. Additional discovery would not be required merely to decide an abstract legal question, but Appellants asserted that discovery would bear on Stark's role in the foreclosure, control, breach, and causation. Thus harmlessness cannot be established simply by quoting Steele. The advocate risks losing the procedural affirmance unless the court first agrees that every pleaded theory fails on its face.
challenges.suggested_response: The trial court’s error was not harmless. The court resolved the motion by relying on a foreclosure-sale fact not alleged in the pleadings, and Appellants had specifically requested discovery under Civ.R. 56(F) to depose Stark and develop evidence concerning duty, breach, causation, and Stark’s relationship to the foreclosing party. Because the court did not confine itself to the pleadings, and because the requested discovery went directly to issues material to liability, the matter should have been treated under Civ.R. 56 and held in abeyance for discovery before any final ruling.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not concede harmlessness. Argue that the trial court relied on a foreclosure-sale fact outside the pleadings and that Appellants’ Civ.R. 56(F) affidavit identified specific discovery needed on duty, breach, causation, and Stark’s relationship to the foreclosing party, so the error affected the disposition.

attacks_proposed.argument: The complaint's causation allegations are conclusory and do not plausibly connect Stark's 2005 failure to abate with the child's lead poisoning years later, after multiple intervening owners. Proximate cause requires a reasonable connection between the act or omission and the injury. Shroades v. Rental Homes, Inc., 68 Ohio St.2d 20, 25 (1981). The complaint does not allege that the lead hazard remained unchanged or that subsequent owners did not contribute to the condition. At the pleading stage, mere possibility of causation is insufficient; the complaint must contain factual allegations that make causation plausible. The trial court properly dismissed for failure to state a claim.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without adequate causation allegations, even if a duty existed, the negligence claim cannot proceed, and the dismissal was proper.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even under the de novo standard of review limited to the pleadings, the complaint fails to state a claim because it does not allege that Stark owed a duty to the Carters after transferring the property. The standard of review does not alter the substantive legal deficiency. Thus, any error in the trial court's consideration of outside materials is harmless, and the dismissal should be affirmed.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the complaint is legally insufficient on its face, the standard of review argument does not change the outcome, and the appellate court will not reverse.

The lack of controlling Ohio authority is nevertheless a serious obstacle, and if the court declines to adopt the proposed Restatement rule, the common-law theory fails.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly acknowledges that no Ohio case has adopted or interpreted § 840A, but relies on DiCenzo for Ohio courts' use of the Restatement, Olpp for continuing-nuisance principles, and Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania, and New Hampshire authorities recognizing some post-transfer nuisance liability. It alleges that Stark knew of the hazard, failed to abate it, concealed it, and transferred or abandoned the property with the nuisance continuing.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full opinions in Steele v. McNatt, Wiles v. Miller, and DiCenzo, along with Ohio decisions addressing former-owner liability for conditions existing at transfer, would determine whether Steele's quoted language applies to accrued tort liability and whether Ohio has accepted analogous Restatement principles.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack lands strongly as to R.C. 5321.04: the statutory text quoted by the brief applies to a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement, and Stark was not the Carters' landlord during their tenancy. Shroades and Sikora therefore do not by themselves extend that statute's negligence-per-se duty to later tenants after title has passed. Still, the brief cites no controlling Ohio authority holding that these lead-abatement provisions create a tort duty running from a former owner to subsequent occupants. That missing legal bridge is a substantial merits problem.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that C.C.O. 240.04(e) imposes a specific command not to disobey a control order, that R.C. 3742.37 and related regulations protect children under six, and that Stark violated the order while it owned the property. It invokes Shroades, Sikora, Swoboda, and Ornella for negligence per se and argues that contractual privity is unnecessary. It does not identify an Ohio case extending these provisions to injuries suffered by occupants who arrived after Stark ceased being landlord.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The operative 2004-2006 versions of C.C.O. Chapter 240, R.C. 3742.37-.38, and R.C. 5321.04, plus Ohio cases addressing whether lead-control orders support negligence per se or an implied civil duty to later occupants, would settle the scope and protected class questions.

judge_assessments.assessment: A harmless-error argument is available, but this version depends entirely on establishing as a matter of law that no post-transfer duty could exist. Source 73 does not support that categorical premise; its snippet quotes Steele's divestiture language but immediately identifies a qualification or unresolved issue when a selling landlord has already failed to remedy a statutory defect. The record also indicates that the trial court affirmatively relied on the foreclosure manner of transfer, a fact different from the pleaded direct sale. If that fact was outside the pleadings, the court could not use it while granting Civ.R. 12(B)(6) relief without following the appropriate conversion procedure. Additional discovery would not be required merely to decide an abstract legal question, but Appellants asserted that discovery would bear on Stark's role in the foreclosure, control, breach, and causation. Thus harmlessness cannot be established simply by quoting Steele. The advocate risks losing the procedural affirmance unless the court first agrees that every pleaded theory fails on its face.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that Stark relied on discovery responses, that the trial court relied on an unpleaded foreclosure fact, and that the motion therefore should have been treated under Civ.R. 56. It also says the Civ.R. 56(F) affidavit identified an unattended corporate deposition and sought facts concerning duty, breach, causation, Stark's financial relationship with the foreclosing party, and whether foreclosure was deliberately allowed. Separately, it argues that R.C. 5302.30's foreclosure disclosure exemption governs buyer-seller disclosure and does not eliminate all tort duties to injured third parties.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The motion, attached discovery responses, judgment entry, Civ.R. 56(F) affidavit, and full Steele opinion are needed to determine whether outside materials were actually considered, whether conversion notice was required, and whether the proposed discovery could affect a legally viable claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source supports only the general requirement of a reasonable causal connection; it does not support the attack's asserted federal-style plausibility standard or a requirement that the complaint negate intervening causes. Ohio pleading law applicable to this 2011 appeal used the Civ.R. 12(B)(6) no-set-of-facts framework invoked by both the trial court and the brief. The pleadings allege a lead hazard at the same property, Stark's actual notice and failure to abate it, continuation of the condition, the child's later exposure there, and resulting lead poisoning. Those allegations may ultimately be difficult to prove after intervening ownership, but they provide more than a bare assertion at the pleading stage. The causation gap is principally an evidentiary issue unless the legal-duty theory fails first.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes allegations that defendants' failure to remove or cover lead-containing paint, dust, and soil caused the injuries; alleges Stark received and violated a lead-hazard order; states that a later owner received a similar order; and argues that causation is inferential and ordinarily for the jury. It also recognizes that proximate cause must ultimately be proved.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The exact complaint and controlling Ohio pleading decisions in effect in 2011 would confirm the required factual specificity. Later evidence concerning the property's condition and other exposure sources would matter at summary judgment or trial, not ordinarily on Civ.R. 12(B)(6).

judge_assessments.assessment: It is correct that de novo review does not cure a substantive failure to state a claim, but the attack misdescribes the pleadings. The complaint expressly alleges that the city orders created a legal duty to third parties, that Stark breached duties owed to subsequent occupants, and that the breach caused injury. Whether Ohio law recognizes those alleged duties is a serious legal issue addressed by attacks a2 and a3; it is not an absence of an allegation. Nor does the conclusion that outside-material error was harmless follow unless all statutory and common-law theories are first rejected on their face. As framed, this adds nothing independent to the stronger duty arguments.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief pleads and argues both a statutory negligence-per-se duty and a common-law duty to subsequent occupants, while acknowledging that Ohio has not previously recognized this precise former-owner theory. It also argues that the foreclosure disclosure exemption does not dispose of duties owed to injured third parties.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: No separate research is necessary beyond the authority identified for attacks a2 and a3.

results.verdict: partly persuasive but exposed on the core duty theory
results.assessment: The brief has its best footing in arguing that R.C. 5321.04 does not fit a former owner who was not the landlord, and it usefully presses the Civ.R. 56(F) / conversion problem because the trial court appears to have relied on a foreclosure fact outside the pleadings. But it is vulnerable on the main merits point: Ohio has no controlling authority adopting the Restatement rules the brief leans on, and the strongest challenge is the missing legal bridge tying the lead-hazard order and ordinance to a duty running from a former owner to later occupants. The brief also overstates Steele if it treats transfer as wiping out all liability. The research leaves the former-owner duty issue unsettled only in the narrow sense that no controlling Ohio case squarely resolves it...

challenges.opponent_argument: Appellants’ reliance on Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 840A and 373 is misplaced because those sections address conditions that constitute a nuisance to persons outside the land, not injuries to subsequent occupants of the same land. The lead hazard here is a condition on the premises that allegedly harmed a later tenant, not a nuisance affecting neighboring property. Ohio courts have not extended these Restatement provisions to the landlord-tenant context, and the general rule of non-liability after transfer (source 39) should control.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the Restatement sections are inapplicable, the common law nuisance theory fails, and the dismissal should be upheld.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest merits attack. Section 373 expressly concerns unreasonable risks to persons outside the land, while the Carters allege exposure as later occupants of the premises. Section 840A likewise speaks in nuisance terms and the quoted comment describes responsibility toward persons outside the land. Source 39 does not establish this limitation, but the Restatement language reproduced in the brief itself exposes it. Unless Ohio authority extends these sections to later occupants, the brief may have selected the wrong common-law doctrine. The advocate risks losing the principal theory offered to carry liability beyond transfer.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee reads Sections 840A and 373 too narrowly and too literally. The point of those provisions is not limited to harm to neighboring land; it is that a party who creates or knowingly leaves in place a dangerous condition does not automatically escape responsibility by transferring the property. Here, the Third Party Complaint alleges that Stark received a lawful lead-hazard order, failed to remediate the condition while it controlled the premises, and then transferred the property without abating the danger. The cited Restatement provisions are offered as persuasive support for the principle that transfer does not erase liability for a hazard the seller itself created or left uncorrected.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that Sections 840A and 373 are not a perfect factual fit and stop treating them as if they directly govern injuries to later occupants. Use them only, if at all, as analogies for the broader principle that a creator of a hazardous condition cannot avoid responsibility simply by transferring title.

challenges.opponent_argument: The common law nuisance and continuing liability theory is not recognized in Ohio for lead-paint claims against a former owner. The Restatement sections cited by Appellants have not been adopted by Ohio courts in this context, and Ohio law generally holds that a former owner’s obligations cease upon transfer. Source 39 confirms that ‘prior owners of a rental property are divested of all rights and obligations to the said property on the date the title to the property is transferred.’ The out-of-state cases and Restatement provisions do not override this settled Ohio rule.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a recognized duty after transfer, the nuisance-based claim cannot survive a motion to dismiss, and the trial court’s ruling should be affirmed.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands as a substantial but not dispositive objection. Source 39 supports an Ohio baseline that former owners ordinarily lose property-related rights and obligations upon transfer, and the brief concedes that Ohio has not adopted Section 840A in this setting. The attack overstates the baseline, however, by treating it as necessarily extinguishing liability for a tort committed during ownership or for a nuisance the former owner created or concealed. Those are the very exceptions the Restatement and the brief's authorities attempt to establish. At the pleading stage, the absence of an already decided Ohio lead-paint case does not itself require dismissal, but the advocate risks asking an intermediate court to recognize a materially new duty without controlling Ohio precedent.
challenges.suggested_response: Ohio law generally provides that a prior owner is divested of the property’s rights and obligations upon transfer, but that baseline does not answer whether a former owner may be liable for a tort it committed while owning the premises. The Third Party Complaint alleges that Stark knowingly left a hazardous lead condition unremediated after notice and a lawful order to abate, and then transferred the property without correcting the danger. The authorities cited above are offered only to show that a vendor who creates or knowingly leaves behind a dangerous condition is not necessarily insulated from liability merely by passing title; they do not depend on a new post-transfer duty arising from ownership alone.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not present Ohio as having already recognized a free-standing post-transfer nuisance cause of action for lead paint. Recast the Restatement and out-of-state authorities as persuasive support only for liability arising from Stark’s own creation or concealment of the hazard before transfer.

challenges.opponent_argument: The negligence per se theory fails because Stark Group owed no duty under R.C. 5321.04 or the cited Cleveland ordinances after it transferred ownership of the property. Ohio law is clear that, absent an agreement or statute to the contrary, a prior owner is divested of all rights and obligations upon transfer of title. See Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law (source 39), citing Steele v. McNatt. The lead hazard control order was directed to Stark as the owner at that time; once it sold the property, the obligation to abate passed to the new owner. The statutes and ordinances do not impose a continuing duty on a former owner for the benefit of future unknown occupants.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Stark had no duty, the negligence per se claim collapses, and the trial court’s dismissal was proper as a matter of law.
