challenges.judge_assessment: The cited authority supports the limited legal proposition that open and obvious is not a defense to a properly supported negligence-per-se claim under specified provisions of R.C. 5321.04. It does not make Armstrong inapplicable to Friese's common-law premises-liability claim, and it does not establish that Baker violated any statutory duty here. On this record, the attack is contingent on Friese first identifying an applicable statutory or code duty, most plausibly under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1). Baker's A(2) argument does not answer an A(1) claim, but the record presently described does not establish one. Friese therefore cannot obtain a trial merely by citing Mann and Robinson; Baker risks losing only the breadth of her open-and-obvious defense if a viable statutory claim is properly raised.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese’s Complaint alleges only that he was a business invitee and that the stairway was defective because it lacked a railing; it does not plead a negligence-per-se claim under R.C. 5321.04, nor does the record identify any applicable code provision. Accordingly, the claim actually before the Court is governed by the common-law premises-liability rule in Armstrong v. Best Buy Co., Inc., 99 Ohio St.3d 79, 2003-Ohio-2573, and the open-and-obvious nature of the stairway remains a complete defense to that claim. Mann and Robinson are inapposite because Friese has not properly placed a statutory R.C. 5321.04 theory before the Court.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the open-and-obvious section to make clear that Baker is addressing the common-law invitee claim actually pleaded, not a statutory negligence-per-se claim. The brief should say that Friese did not plead or support an R.C. 5321.04 claim, so Mann and Robinson do not displace Armstrong here.

challenges.opponent_argument: The personal injury claim is not a compulsory counterclaim because it does not arise from the same transaction or occurrence as the prior eviction and damages action. The compulsory counterclaim rule requires that the claim 'arises out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the opposing party's claim.' Civ.R. 13(A). The prior action was for back rent and property damage, while this action is for personal injuries from a fall that occurred months earlier. The mere fact that both involve the tenancy does not make them the same transaction or occurrence. The brief's reliance on Sherman v. Pearson is distinguishable because there the injury occurred in a common area and was directly related to the landlord's maintenance duties that were also at issue in the eviction. Here, the fall was inside the rented premises and unrelated to the non-payment of rent or property damage. Moreover, the Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law treatise notes that if the eviction complaint alleges only a claim for possession, Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply, and even when a money claim is included, the tenant's claim must still arise from the same transaction. The brief fails to establish that the personal injury claim and the back rent claim are part of the same transaction or occurrence.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the personal injury claim is not a compulsory counterclaim, res judicata does not bar it, and the case may proceed.

challenges.judge_assessment: The general same-transaction objection is legally available, but the proposed distinctions do not overcome the authorities Baker actually cites. The prior case was not possession-only; its monetary claim proceeded to judgment. The cited treatise therefore does not help Friese on its possession-only exception. Baker also cites Adams as involving a tenant's fall down steps followed by a landlord's eviction-and-damages action, and Sherman expressly treated tenancy-based maintenance and rent claims as logically related. The proposed assertion that maintenance duties were also litigated in Sherman, or that a common-area fall is materially different from a fall within leased premises, is unsupported by the supplied authority. Friese would risk minimizing close adverse precedent. A narrower, record-specific challenge to the logical relationship might be arguable, but this attack does not develop it.
challenges.suggested_response: Baker’s prior municipal-court action was not limited to possession; it included a claim for monetary damages, and that damages claim proceeded to trial and final judgment. (Exs. B, C). Friese’s present claim arises from the same tenancy relationship and the same rented premises, so it was a logically related claim that Civ.R. 13(A) required him to assert in the prior action. See Sherman v. Pearson, 110 Ohio App.3d 70, 75, 673 N.E.2d 643 (1996). Because Friese did not assert any such claim before judgment was entered in Baker’s favor, his present action is barred by res judicata.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the res judicata theory, but trim the overreach and lean on the record that Baker’s municipal action included a damages claim that was tried to final judgment. Avoid arguing from the possession-only exception, and focus on the logical relation between the tenancy-based injury claim and the prior damages action.

A missing handrail may violate such codes, as recognized in McHugh v. Zataar, No. 14-CA-010591, 2015 WL 7273177 (Ohio App., 9th Dist., Jan. 20, 2015) (city code, duty to install handrail on basement stairway). The cases cited by Baker, St. Germain and Taylor, address only the habitability duty under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2), not the separate duty under (A)(1). Therefore, there is a genuine issue of material fact as to whether a handrail was required by applicable codes, precluding summary judgment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) imposes a duty to install a handrail, Baker's argument that no statutory duty exists fails, and summary judgment must be denied.

attacks_proposed.argument: The personal injury claim is not a compulsory counterclaim because it does not arise from the same transaction or occurrence as the prior eviction and damages action. The compulsory counterclaim rule requires that the claim 'arises out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the opposing party's claim.' Civ.R. 13(A). The prior action was for back rent and property damage, while this action is for personal injuries from a fall that occurred months earlier. The mere fact that both involve the tenancy does not make them the same transaction or occurrence. The brief's reliance on Sherman v. Pearson is distinguishable because there the injury occurred in a common area and was directly related to the landlord's maintenance duties that were also at issue in the eviction. Here, the fall was inside the rented premises and unrelated to the non-payment of rent or property damage. Moreover, the Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law treatise notes that if the eviction complaint alleges only a claim for possession, Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply, and even when a money claim is included, the tenant's claim must still arise from the same transaction. The brief fails to establish that the personal injury claim and the back rent claim are part of the same transaction or occurrence.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the personal injury claim is not a compulsory counterclaim, res judicata does not bar it, and the case may proceed.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief assumes that the absence of a handrail is the relevant hazard and that it was open and obvious. However, the open and obvious doctrine requires that the specific hazard be observable. Friese testified that he was aware of the staircase and the lack of a handrail, but he also testified that he fell because he was turning to close the door and lost his balance. The hazard may have been the combination of the missing handrail and the need to turn while descending, which is not open and obvious. The brief fails to address whether the specific danger that caused the fall—the need to negotiate the door while stepping down without a handrail—was open and obvious. This is a factual issue for the jury.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the specific hazard was not open and obvious, the open and obvious doctrine does not bar the claim, and summary judgment must be denied.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief asserts that Friese moved out voluntarily after the eviction action was filed, but the record does not support this. The case record only shows that the eviction action was filed and that judgment was entered for Baker. There is no evidence that Friese moved out voluntarily; he may have been evicted. This fact is material because if the eviction claim was resolved by eviction rather than voluntary move-out, the nature of the prior action might affect the res judicata analysis. The brief's unsupported assertion cannot be the basis for summary judgment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the prior action involved an eviction rather than a voluntary move-out, the res judicata analysis may differ, and summary judgment is inappropriate on this record.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes a real overstatement in Baker's motion: the cited handrail cases address habitability under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2), while R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) separately incorporates applicable safety codes, and the cited source identifies a case recognizing a code-based basement-handrail duty. But the attack does not identify any code applicable to this Thompson property or place evidence of a violation in the record. McHugh is also Ninth District authority, not controlling in Geauga County. Thus the attack undermines Baker's categorical assertion that Ohio law can never impose a handrail duty, but it does not by itself create a genuine issue or require denial of summary judgment. Friese stands to lose the statutory theory unless he supplies the applicable code and shows that it materially affects health and safety.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Friese pleaded only invitee premises liability, not a statutory claim, and relies on St. Germain and Taylor to argue that a missing handrail does not violate the fit-and-habitable duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(2). It does not address the distinct code-compliance duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(1).
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Determine which state or local building code governed this basement stairway on January 16, 2021, whether it required a handrail, whether it applied to an existing structure, and whether the complaint and Civ.R. 56 materials adequately raised that theory.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited authority supports the limited legal proposition that open and obvious is not a defense to a properly supported negligence-per-se claim under specified provisions of R.C. 5321.04. It does not make Armstrong inapplicable to Friese's common-law premises-liability claim, and it does not establish that Baker violated any statutory duty here. On this record, the attack is contingent on Friese first identifying an applicable statutory or code duty, most plausibly under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1). Baker's A(2) argument does not answer an A(1) claim, but the record presently described does not establish one. Friese therefore cannot obtain a trial merely by citing Mann and Robinson; Baker risks losing only the breadth of her open-and-obvious defense if a viable statutory claim is properly raised.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief applies Armstrong to the pleaded invitee claim and separately argues that a missing handrail does not violate the habitability duty under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2). It also says the complaint did not allege a landlord-statutory theory. It does not acknowledge that open and obvious is unavailable against certain R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claims.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the complaint under Ohio notice-pleading standards and determine whether an R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) or (A)(3) claim was fairly pleaded and supported by an identified code violation or common-area evidence.

judge_assessments.assessment: The general same-transaction objection is legally available, but the proposed distinctions do not overcome the authorities Baker actually cites. The prior case was not possession-only; its monetary claim proceeded to judgment. The cited treatise therefore does not help Friese on its possession-only exception. Baker also cites Adams as involving a tenant's fall down steps followed by a landlord's eviction-and-damages action, and Sherman expressly treated tenancy-based maintenance and rent claims as logically related. The proposed assertion that maintenance duties were also litigated in Sherman, or that a common-area fall is materially different from a fall within leased premises, is unsupported by the supplied authority. Friese would risk minimizing close adverse precedent. A narrower, record-specific challenge to the logical relationship might be arguable, but this attack does not develop it.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief applies Civ.R. 13(A)'s logical-relation test, cites several tenant-injury and landlord-damages cases, and emphasizes that Baker's prior monetary claim proceeded to trial and final judgment. It argues both claims arose from rights and duties generated by the tenancy.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual complaints and full opinions in Adams, Sherman, Haney, and Maduka would determine whether the prior property-damage allegations and this stairway injury share operative facts beyond the general tenancy relationship.

judge_assessments.assessment: The record does not support recasting the hazard as an undisclosed combination of the door, turning movement, and missing handrail. Friese described his own movement as the assumed cause of losing balance, while the complaint identified the missing railing and he admittedly knew of it. He had also used the same entrance several times daily for nearly four years, which makes the door configuration and required turn at least as familiar as the stairs. Without authority or evidence showing a concealed condition or legally sufficient attendant circumstance, this does not create a jury issue over whether the identified hazard was observable. Pressing it risks substituting a new hazard theory for the one pleaded.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies the alleged hazard as the missing handrail, notes that Friese had previously told Baker a railing was needed, and relies on his years of frequent use, lighting, and knowledge of the unchanged staircase. It also quotes his testimony that he was turning to close the outward-opening door when he lost balance.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Evidence of unusual stair geometry, code violations, visual concealment, or an external attendant circumstance—and Ohio authority applying attendant-circumstances doctrine to a similar doorway-stair configuration—could change the analysis.

judge_assessments.assessment: Even if the assertion that Friese moved voluntarily lacks a proper Civ.R. 56 citation, it is not material to Baker's preclusion theory. Baker relies on the municipal court's monetary-damages claim proceeding to judgment, not on how the possession claim ended. Whether Friese left voluntarily or under an eviction order does not determine whether his injury claim was compulsory in response to the damages claim. The court would not deny summary judgment over this collateral factual dispute, and emphasizing it would distract from the material same-transaction issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Friese moved voluntarily after filing, but separately states that Baker's second cause of action for monetary damages proceeded to trial and judgment. Its res judicata conclusion rests on that damages judgment.

judge_assessments.assessment: This reverses the burdens and misreads the motion. Baker did not assume the burden of proving reasonable notice and an opportunity to repair merely by arguing that R.C. 5321.04 supplies no handrail duty. Notice or opportunity to cure would ordinarily be part of Friese's effort to establish liability where the governing duty requires it. Moreover, the complaint allegedly states that Friese told Baker the staircase needed a railing, so the brief does contain a notice allegation even though it gives no date. This is not a missing element of Baker's summary-judgment defense.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that no statutory handrail duty exists and quotes the complaint's allegation that Friese told Baker the staircase needed a railing.

judge_assessments.assessment: Baker was not required to plead the statutory remedy Friese seeks. She is the defendant seeking judgment against his personal-injury complaint, and the alleged consequence is already apparent: damages for injuries from the fall. Invoking R.C. 5321.04 defensively did not obligate Baker to establish abatement, a defense to possession, or another tenant remedy. The court would not reach this objection, and advancing it would confuse liability with remedies.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief characterizes the action as one seeking compensation for injuries sustained in the fall and argues that neither common law nor R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) supplies the asserted duty.

results.assessment: The motion reads coherently on the common-law premises-liability theory and its res judicata framing, but it overstates the handrail issue and leaves the key statutory question underdeveloped. The biggest weakness is that the handrail argument relies on cases about habitability while not addressing the separate code-based duty under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1), and the record as described does not identify an applicable code or violation. The open-and-obvious argument is also only strong if no viable statutory claim is in play. On preclusion, Baker has better support than Friese’s attack admits, but the counterclaim analysis still turns on the logical-relationship record, which the brief does not fully pin down.

challenges.judge_assessment: The legal principle is sound but the attack lacks a record predicate. Source 4 indicates that a proven violation of R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) can constitute negligence per se and displace the open-and-obvious doctrine. Nothing identified here, however, establishes that this interior staircase was a statutory common area, that any applicable code required a handrail, or that Friese pleaded and supported such a statutory claim. A possibility that the stairs “may” violate an unidentified provision does not create a Civ.R. 56 issue. Without code text, applicability evidence, and a properly presented statutory theory, this court would not deny summary judgment on that basis. The opponent risks distracting from stronger issues by presenting a legally valid exception without facts to invoke it.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese has not identified any record evidence that R.C. 5321.04(A)(3), any building code, or any other statutory duty applies to these stairs. The Complaint pleads a common-law premises-liability theory, and nothing in the summary-judgment record establishes a statutory violation. On this record, the Court should apply the governing common-law open-and-obvious rule, which bars Friese’s claim.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not try to concede or supply a statutory negligence-per-se theory without a record basis. Keep the argument on the record as pleaded: Friese has not identified any statute, code provision, or admissible evidence showing that the stairway falls within an exception to the open-and-obvious rule.

challenges.opponent_argument: The open and obvious doctrine applies only when the danger itself is open and obvious, not merely the condition. Friese's knowledge that there was no handrail does not establish that the danger of falling due to the absence of a handrail was open and obvious. The brief conflates knowledge of the condition with knowledge of the danger. The record shows Friese testified he was careful and didn't notice anything unusual, but that does not prove the danger was objectively obvious. Thus, a genuine issue of material fact exists.
challenges.why_it_matters: Prevents summary judgment because the open-and-obvious determination is a factual question for the jury.

challenges.judge_assessment: The condition-versus-danger distinction does not generate a material factual dispute on this record. Ohio's doctrine covers dangers known to the invitee as well as those objectively observable. Friese allegedly told Baker that the staircase needed a railing, which supports not merely awareness of the missing railing but recognition of the associated safety concern. His statement that nothing appeared unusual on the day of the fall is consistent with the brief's position that the unchanged condition was long known to him. The attack also overstates the rule by treating open-and-obvious status invariably as a jury question. The opponent would gain little and risk emphasizing Friese's admission of prior knowledge.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese’s own testimony defeats any claim of a hidden danger. He used the basement stairs three to four times a day for nearly four years, testified that he was well aware of their condition and was careful in using them, and alleged in his Complaint that he had told Baker the staircase needed a railing. That is not merely knowledge that a handrail was absent; it is an admission that he understood the safety concern now complained of. Under Armstrong and the open-and-obvious doctrine, Baker owed no duty to warn of a danger that Friese already knew about.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strengthen the existing open-and-obvious analysis by tying Friese’s admissions to actual knowledge of the risk, not just the physical condition. Do not rest the point on visibility alone; rest it on his repeated use, his caution, and his statement that the staircase needed a railing.

The logical relation test is not satisfied: the injury claim involves a separate tort occurring months before the eviction filing, with different evidence and legal issues. The brief's reliance on Sherman v. Pearson is distinguishable because there the injury occurred in a common area during the tenancy and was directly related to the landlord's maintenance duties under the lease. Here, the fall was in Friese's own apartment and not part of the dispute over rent and damages. See Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law § 2 (source 22) discussing that not all claims are compulsory.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the claim is not a compulsory counterclaim, res judicata does not bar it, and the prior judgment has no preclusive effect.

record_sources.quote:
"On May 25, 2021, Baker filed an eviction action, which also included a claim for both back rent and for damage to the premises... The second cause of action proceeded to trial on July 21, 2021, at which Friese did not appear. The trial court took evidence and granted judgment in favor of Baker for the sum of $5,336.00 together with statutory interest and court costs."

"In the case sub judice, Friese's alleged injuries occurred on January 16, 2021... Friese admits in his Complaint that his status as an \"invitee\" arises because of his tenancy relationship with Baker."

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack runs against the brief's most factually analogous cited authorities. Adams and Sherman, as described in the brief, involved tenants' stairway-injury claims followed by landlord actions seeking possession and monetary relief, and held the injury claims compulsory under the logical-relation test. Source 22 principally supports an exception when the earlier action seeks possession only; Baker's earlier complaint also sought monetary damages and proceeded to judgment on that claim. The distinctions between a common-area staircase and a staircase serving Friese's apartment, and between maintenance evidence and rent evidence, do not overcome the cited holdings that tenancy-based duties can supply the required logical relation. The opponent risks conceding the controlling analogy while offering distinctions the cited rule does not make material.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese’s personal-injury claim was a compulsory counterclaim in Baker’s prior municipal-court action because it arose out of the same tenancy relationship and the same premises. Baker’s complaint did not seek possession alone; it also sought monetary damages arising from the tenancy, and that damages claim proceeded to trial and final judgment. Under Civ.R. 13(A) and the authorities cited above, Friese was required to assert his claim in that action, and his failure to do so bars this later suit under res judicata.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Reframe the res judicata point around Civ.R. 13(A) and the fact that Baker’s prior municipal-court case sought both eviction and money damages. Do not overstate the analogy; anchor it in the tenancy-based relationship and the final damages judgment already in the record.

attacks_proposed.argument: The open and obvious doctrine does not bar Friese's claim because the absence of a handrail may violate R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) or applicable building codes, which constitutes negligence per se and obviates the open-and-obvious doctrine. See Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law § 4.b (source 4). The brief fails to address this statutory duty, so its argument is legally insufficient.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court finds a statutory violation, the open-and-obvious defense fails, and Baker's motion must be denied.

attacks_proposed.argument: The open and obvious doctrine applies only when the danger itself is open and obvious, not merely the condition. Friese's knowledge that there was no handrail does not establish that the danger of falling due to the absence of a handrail was open and obvious. The brief conflates knowledge of the condition with knowledge of the danger. The record shows Friese testified he was careful and didn't notice anything unusual, but that does not prove the danger was objectively obvious. Thus, a genuine issue of material fact exists.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Prevents summary judgment because the open-and-obvious determination is a factual question for the jury.

attacks_proposed.argument: The compulsory counterclaim rule does not apply because the personal injury claim does not arise out of the same transaction or occurrence as Baker's eviction and damages action. The logical relation test is not satisfied: the injury claim involves a separate tort occurring months before the eviction filing, with different evidence and legal issues. The brief's reliance on Sherman v. Pearson is distinguishable because there the injury occurred in a common area during the tenancy and was directly related to the landlord's maintenance duties under the lease. Here, the fall was in Friese's own apartment and not part of the dispute over rent and damages. See Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law § 2 (source 22) discussing that not all claims are compulsory.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the claim is not a compulsory counterclaim, res judicata does not bar it, and the prior judgment has no preclusive effect.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Chardon Municipal Court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over Friese's personal injury claim if it exceeded the municipal court's monetary limit (R.C. 1901.17, $15,000). A compulsory counterclaim cannot be asserted in a court that lacks jurisdiction over it. The brief does not establish that Friese's claim was within the jurisdictional limit, so it cannot be deemed a compulsory counterclaim. See Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law § 2 (source 40) on municipal court jurisdiction.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the municipal court lacked jurisdiction, the claim could not have been brought there, so res judicata does not bar it.

attacks_proposed.argument: Baker has not met her initial burden under Civ.R. 56 to demonstrate the absence of genuine issues of material fact. The evidence she relies on—Friese's deposition—actually raises factual disputes about whether the staircase was dangerous and whether the absence of a handrail was open and obvious. Construing the evidence in Friese's favor, as required on summary judgment, a reasonable jury could find that the danger was not open and obvious. See CMHA v. Barry Gauntt (source 50) for summary judgment standard.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Denial of summary judgment because the movant failed to carry her burden.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if the condition was open and obvious, a landlord still owes a duty to maintain the premises in a reasonably safe condition, which may include installing handrails as required by law. The open and obvious doctrine only eliminates the duty to warn, not the duty to maintain. The brief incorrectly asserts that Baker owed no duty at all. See Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law § 2 (source 2) (duty to warn vs. duty to maintain).
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if the open-and-obvious doctrine applies, Baker may still be liable for failing to maintain safe premises, so summary judgment is improper.

attacks_proposed.argument: The prior municipal court judgment was a default judgment on Baker's claim for rent and damages; it did not adjudicate Friese's personal injury claim on the merits. Res judicata requires a final judgment on the merits, and a default judgment on a different cause of action does not preclude a later claim that was not actually litigated. The brief's reliance on Love v. O'Donnell is misplaced because that case involved claims that could have been litigated, but here the claim could not have been litigated due to jurisdictional limits and lack of logical relation.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Res judicata does not bar the claim, so the motion fails.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal principle is sound but the attack lacks a record predicate. Source 4 indicates that a proven violation of R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) can constitute negligence per se and displace the open-and-obvious doctrine. Nothing identified here, however, establishes that this interior staircase was a statutory common area, that any applicable code required a handrail, or that Friese pleaded and supported such a statutory claim. A possibility that the stairs “may” violate an unidentified provision does not create a Civ.R. 56 issue. Without code text, applicability evidence, and a properly presented statutory theory, this court would not deny summary judgment on that basis. The opponent risks distracting from stronger issues by presenting a legally valid exception without facts to invoke it.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief treats the claim solely as common-law premises liability and argues under Armstrong that Baker had no duty because the absence of a handrail was observable and actually known. It does not address R.C. 5321.04 or any building code.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complaint, local building code applicable to Thompson Township in January 2021, evidence concerning when the stairs were constructed, and evidence showing whether the staircase was a common area would determine whether this theory is available.

judge_assessments.assessment: The condition-versus-danger distinction does not generate a material factual dispute on this record. Ohio's doctrine covers dangers known to the invitee as well as those objectively observable. Friese allegedly told Baker that the staircase needed a railing, which supports not merely awareness of the missing railing but recognition of the associated safety concern. His statement that nothing appeared unusual on the day of the fall is consistent with the brief's position that the unchanged condition was long known to him. The attack also overstates the rule by treating open-and-obvious status invariably as a jury question. The opponent would gain little and risk emphasizing Friese's admission of prior knowledge.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly argues that Friese used the stairs three to four times daily for nearly four years, knew there was no handrail, and had told Baker that a railing was needed. It relies on both objective observability and actual knowledge, not merely visibility of the physical condition.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Photographs, measurements, and the complete deposition could matter if Friese identifies a distinct, concealed stair defect rather than the known absence of a handrail.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack runs against the brief's most factually analogous cited authorities. Adams and Sherman, as described in the brief, involved tenants' stairway-injury claims followed by landlord actions seeking possession and monetary relief, and held the injury claims compulsory under the logical-relation test. Source 22 principally supports an exception when the earlier action seeks possession only; Baker's earlier complaint also sought monetary damages and proceeded to judgment on that claim. The distinctions between a common-area staircase and a staircase serving Friese's apartment, and between maintenance evidence and rent evidence, do not overcome the cited holdings that tenancy-based duties can supply the required logical relation. The opponent risks conceding the controlling analogy while offering distinctions the cited rule does not make material.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites Adams, Haney, Maduka, Lujan, and Sherman and specifically quotes Sherman's conclusion that claims involving rights and duties arising from the rental relationship satisfy the logical-relation test. It also establishes that Baker sought monetary damages, not possession alone.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full municipal-court complaint and the complete opinions in Adams and Sherman would confirm whether Baker's damages claims concerned conditions or obligations sufficiently related to the injury claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source establishes only that municipal courts have limited jurisdiction; it does not support the proposition that an otherwise compulsory counterclaim exceeding the monetary limit could not be asserted. Ohio procedure provides a mechanism for certification or transfer when a counterclaim exceeds a lower court's jurisdiction. In addition, this record does not establish that Friese's claim necessarily exceeded the applicable limit. The brief need not disprove an unsubstantiated jurisdictional hypothetical in its opening motion. Raising this attack without addressing the transfer mechanism would expose a significant legal omission and could damage credibility.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief assumes that Friese was obligated to assert the injury claim in municipal court but does not discuss the monetary limit or transfer procedure.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The amount demanded in Friese's complaint and the Ohio rule governing transfer or certification of counterclaims exceeding municipal-court jurisdiction would conclusively resolve the point.

judge_assessments.assessment: Source 50 supports the ordinary summary-judgment burden, but the attack does not identify a concrete disputed fact material to either dispositive defense. Baker points to deposition testimony concerning years of daily stair use, unchanged conditions, lighting, and the mechanics of the fall, plus certified records of the prior action. Whether those facts establish no duty or preclusion is primarily a legal question. A generic assertion that a jury could deem the stairs dangerous does not answer actual knowledge or the separate res judicata ground. The opponent risks substituting the summary-judgment standard for a developed response to the motion's evidence.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies Friese's deposition and certified municipal-court records, states the relevant testimony, and argues that Friese's own admissions establish actual knowledge and the facts supporting preclusion.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete deposition, photographs, expert evidence, and any Civ.R. 56 affidavits submitted in opposition would show whether a specific material dispute exists beyond the excerpts quoted.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source does not support the proposed distinction. Source 2 states that when a danger is open and obvious, the landowner owes no duty of care; Armstrong likewise treats the doctrine as eliminating the ordinary premises-liability duty, not merely a duty to warn. A separate statutory negligence-per-se duty may survive, but that is the narrower issue raised in attack a1 and requires proof of an applicable statute or code violation. As framed, this attack misstates Ohio common-law premises liability and would likely be rejected. The advocate risks undermining a potentially viable statutory exception by advancing an overbroad common-law proposition.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on Armstrong for the proposition that an observable or actually known hazard eliminates Baker's duty and concludes that Baker had no duty to warn or install a handrail.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further research would be useful only if Friese pleaded a distinct statutory or contractual maintenance duty; source 2 does not establish that ordinary maintenance duties survive the open-and-obvious doctrine.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack incorrectly treats actual litigation of Friese's injury claim as necessary. Claim preclusion and the compulsory-counterclaim bar extend to claims that could and should have been litigated, and the brief quotes that rule from Love. A judgment entered after a defendant fails to appear can still be a final judgment on the merits for claim-preclusion purposes; the brief also states that the municipal court took evidence and entered judgment, rather than characterizing the disposition as a mere procedural dismissal. The jurisdictional and logical-relation qualifications simply repeat attacks a4 and a3, neither of which is supported on this record. The opponent risks misstating elementary claim-preclusion law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly states that res judicata covers claims that were or could have been litigated, that Baker's monetary claim proceeded to trial, that the court took evidence, and that a final monetary judgment was entered. It then relies on Civ.R. 13(A) rather than issue preclusion requiring actual adjudication of the injury claim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The certified judgment and docket would confirm finality and service, but nothing presently identified suggests that the judgment was vacated, jurisdictionally void, or entered without adjudicating Baker's monetary claim.

results.verdict: generally persuasive, but exposed on the unsupported statuto
results.assessment: As written, the brief has its strongest footing on open and obvious and on the plaintiff’s own admissions of prior knowledge, which undercut any claim that the danger was hidden. Its biggest weakness is that it never squarely addresses, with record support, any statutory or code-based duty that could displace the common-law rule; that point should not be left as a bare possibility. The res judicata section is also vulnerable because it leans on analogies the research did not fully settle, especially where the earlier case sought both possession and damages. The condition-versus-danger objection is the least persuasive attack on the brief.
